factors.description: The request names neither TDD, a runner, nor the skill itself — only a module the owner trusts least and the fact that nothing beside it has a test — so an agent that reaches for unit-testing here is finding it from the problem, with jest-testing (the runner's own mechanics) and end-to-end-testing (a whole-system check of what a reader sees) sitting right there as the two competing readings of the same anxiety; the two skills' own descriptions disclaim each other explicitly, which is what keeps this a real question rather than a formality.

unit-testing requires a callable subject named in a `describe(...)` or case title to carry the `()` suffix, and forbids it on a non-callable one. Every subject `resolve-translation.ts` offers — `normalizeLocale`, `findExactMatch`, `findLanguageMatch`, `resolveTranslation` — is callable, and the one spec already in the tree, `blog-post-slug.spec.ts`, names a schema and is therefore correctly bare, demonstrating only the rule's other half. A control run has nothing local to copy the callable-naming convention from.

unit-testing requires cases sharing a condition to sit under their own nested `describe("when ...")` block. `resolve-translation.ts` has four such conditions by construction — an exact match, a language-only match, a fallback to the post's default locale, and no match at all — and `blog-post-slug.spec.ts` is one flat block of five ungrouped cases, so the codebase demonstrates the opposite of the convention this factor checks for. It judges only whether a condition-named group exists, not how deeply it nests — a limit its own script states.
